episode_title: Why I Am a Free Speech Absolutist

stories.topic: Priyanka Chopra Flopped, the Aghori Baba Went Viral
stories.summary: Amit relays what their friend Roshan Abbas told them at a party at Ajay's house. One week Ranveer Allahbadia (BeerBiceps) released a Priyanka Chopra interview he expected to go viral, and nothing happened. Another episode, with an Aghori Baba, got about two million views in six hours, so he leaned into tantra and Aghori content. Later, ahead of the elections, government ministers including Jaishankar and Piyush Goyal skipped the smaller right-wing podcasts and went on his show for its reach. The left promptly branded him a right-winger. Amit says he was no kind of winger, just a curious host with no ideology who let big names come on.
stories.insight: Creators and politicians both follow the numbers. Ideological labels are often pinned on someone because of who appears on their show, not because of anything they believe.
stories.quote: there was a particular week where BeerBiceps came out with a show on Priyanka Chopra and he thought that's gonna go madly viral and nothing happened, but he came out with another show with a tantric, with an Aghori Baba. And that went madly viral, two million views in six hours or whatever.

stories.topic: Defending the Guy Nobody Will Defend
stories.summary: On Samay's subscription-only show India's Got Latent, Ranveer asked a crude question about parents and incest. Amit points out it wasn't even original: it had been an old Reddit question for twenty years, and a much bigger Indian comedian used it in a show seven years earlier. A clip went viral, the right piled on, and then the state stepped in. Police cases were filed in several places including Assam. The Supreme Court process left him with his passport taken away and an order to produce no more content. Around forty people connected to the show faced cases, including the editor. Amit, who has never watched a full episode of Ranveer's show, tweeted that he was a well-intentioned kid who had apologised gracefully, and that anyone who disliked the content shouldn't watch it. Both left and right attacked Amit for it. His worry is that a hated target lets the state sneak in a broadcast bill through the back door, or simply normalise treating creators this way.
stories.insight: Free speech is tested by the people nobody wants to defend. Once a crackdown is normalised against a disliked target, the same tools can be used on everyone else.
stories.quote: a fundamental principle of free speech is you should defend the people that you disagree with the most.

stories.topic: Section 295A: Beef, Weddings and a Joke Book
stories.summary: Amit recalls a column he wrote around 2007 on how Section 295A (deliberately outraging religious feelings) was being used. Cases were filed against Ravi Shastri for saying on air, during a series in South Africa, that he likes eating beef. Another was filed over Elizabeth Hurley's marriage to Arun Nayar because not all Hindu rituals were performed. Another targeted the publisher of a Santa-Banta joke book. Since such a case can be filed anywhere, the accused may have to keep turning up at a court in, say, Tripura.
stories.insight: Vague speech laws do their damage through the legal process itself, whatever the verdict. Anyone can be dragged across the country over almost anything.
stories.quote: You've got to show up in court. If this is filed in Tripura, you have to go to the court there, et cetera, et cetera. You know the process is a punishment.

stories.topic: How Nehru Amended His Way Past the Courts
stories.summary: In the early 1950s Nehru was cracking down on speech, from the RSS magazine The Organiser to Romesh Thapar's communist magazine Crossroads. The Supreme Court overturned the Crossroads ban, and the sedition law (124A) was struck down. Nehru responded with the First Amendment, adding caveats such as public order and relations with friendly countries. Those caveats later let sedition return. He argued that when the courts block the legislature on basic social matters, the legislature should amend the Constitution. He was opposed by Acharya Kripalani, Jayaprakash Narayan and Syama Prasad Mookerjee, and Naziruddin Ahmad, an MP from Bengal, warned that sedition would come back. Amit admits he once wrongly said the First Amendment itself revived sedition and got corrected, but says it was true in spirit because the amendment laid the grounds.
stories.insight: Even a celebrated liberal, convinced that 'people like me' will use power wisely, will build tools his rivals later inherit. Today the boot is on the other foot, and every party uses these laws.
stories.quote: maybe you will continue for eternity in the next generation for generations unborn. That is quite possible. But supposing some other party comes into authority, what is the precedent you are laying down?

stories.topic: Why Films Get Censored but Books Don't
stories.summary: In 1968 K.A. Abbas made A Tale of Four Cities, a documentary set in Mumbai's red-light districts. The challenge to it went to the Supreme Court, which ruled that cinema needs closer scrutiny than books because a moving image stirs people more deeply. That reasoning underpins film censorship, where a board of bureaucrats decides what Indian society is fit to see.
stories.insight: Censorship rests on a paternalistic view that ordinary people are too impressionable to be trusted. Society has normalised that assumption so fully that it goes unquestioned.
stories.quote: a person reading a book or other writing or hearing a speech or viewing a painting or sculpture is not so deeply stirred as by seeing a motion picture.

stories.topic: 295A Is Bad, Except Against My Enemies
stories.summary: A prominent figure on the left told Amit that 295A and 153A are bad laws. In the same breath, she told a colleague that a 295A case should be filed against a right-wing politician for something he said.
stories.insight: Many self-declared free speech defenders only defend speech they agree with. A principle that switches off for your opponents isn't a principle.
stories.quote: If you agree it is bad, it is bad, period. You can't say that don't use it against us, but I will use it against the enemy.

stories.topic: Satanic Verses Yes, Danish Cartoons No?
stories.summary: Around 2007-08, during the violence over the Danish cartoons, a man Amit calls perhaps the most sensible MP in India today wrote a column. He said he supported Salman Rushdie and The Satanic Verses but not the Danish cartoonists, because the novel was art and the cartoons were mere provocation. Amit rejects the distinction.
stories.insight: Free speech can't depend on whether you rate the work as art or as provocation. The right belongs equally to the masterpiece and to the obnoxious.
stories.quote: You might like Satanic Verses and you might think that what the Danish cartoonists did is absolutely obnoxious and repulsive. That's fine. But both of them have an equal right to free speech.

stories.summary: Amit was recently on a podcast co-hosted by a former guest of The Seen and the Unseen who is close to the Congress party. She said 'we need to uplift the consciousness of the masses.' Amit pushed back: elites should ask whether they are wrong, or why they can't communicate what they think is good, instead of blaming voters as racist or misogynist.
stories.insight: Infantilising the public is an elite habit that runs across parties. In a democracy, the duty to understand and persuade lies with the leaders, not the voters.
stories.quote: No, masses are not the problem, you are the problem.

recommendations.creator: Subhashish Bhadra
recommendations.context: Amit calls it an excellent book while explaining why India's Constitution centralised power.
recommendations.reason: It argues that constitutions are products of their circumstances. America's came from a fight for individual freedom; India's was drafted amid turmoil and fragmentation, so it centralised power and paid only lip service to freedom.

recommendations.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
recommendations.context: Cited right after the Nehru story, as Amit describes how Nehru, Indira and later leaders kept amending the Constitution.
recommendations.reason: Amit says it is a great talk everyone should watch. It shows how amendments became the routine way to make unconstitutional things constitutional.

recommendations.creator: Matt Ridley
recommendations.context: Amit uses Ridley's 'great phrase' to explain the marketplace-of-ideas argument; the talk is linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: It captures why ideas must collide and recombine freely for the best ones to emerge and for society to progress.

recommendations.item: The First Amendment to the US Constitution
recommendations.context: Amit reads it aloud as his gold standard for free speech.
recommendations.reason: 'Congress shall make no law... abridging the freedom of speech' has no caveats. US courts have interpreted it to protect all speech, hate speech included, short of direct incitement to violence, which is exactly where Amit draws his line.

core_ideas.concept: Open on Facts, Firm on Values
core_ideas.explanation: Amit says that after years of thinking, he is all shades of grey on facts, because the world is too complex to understand fully, but black and white on certain values. Free speech is one of those values. Ajay doesn't accept a clean facts/values split. He prefers calibrated, Bayesian confidence: some beliefs need a very big fact to topple them, others only a modest dose.
core_ideas.quote: I have realised that in one domain I am completely about shades of grey and always open to change. In another domain, I am black and white.

core_ideas.concept: Free Speech Absolutism: One Bright Line
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's absolutism follows the US standard. All speech is allowed, including hate speech. The only line is direct incitement to violence, which is already illegal. So 'Gujarati economists shouldn't speak' is protected, while 'here is his address, go lynch him' is not. The deeper reason to be absolute is the question of who decides what is offensive: any gatekeeper you empower today may be your enemy tomorrow.
core_ideas.quote: today the person deciding may be your friend, tomorrow he could be your enemy. And the best way past that is be an absolutist.

core_ideas.explanation: (1) First principles, following John Locke: a newborn owns itself, not the king or the state, and every right flows from self-ownership. Silencing someone denies their personhood and agency. (2) The marketplace of ideas: ideas should compete and recombine (Matt Ridley's 'when ideas have sex'), and an official view can be wrong, so progress usually comes from heretics. (3) Democracy is a contest of ideas about how to run a country. When the state controls information or punishes speech, the result is information asymmetry and a chilling effect, because tomorrow I will think twice before saying the same thing. That is electoral manipulation without touching a ballot box.
core_ideas.quote: Progress comes from heretics. Progress comes from people saying that, you know, the earth goes around the sun and not vice versa, even if the conventional view is different.

core_ideas.concept: Rights Framed from a Police Constable's Point of View
core_ideas.explanation: India's Constitution was drafted amid chaos, with more than 500 princely states and real fear that things would fall apart, so it centralised power. Article 19(1)(a) grants free speech, but 19(2) immediately allows 'reasonable restrictions' on vague grounds like public order, decency and morality, which a police constable gets to interpret. India took over the colonial state, built to rule subjects rather than serve citizens, more or less wholesale: in Amit's words, white-skinned rulers were exchanged for brown-skinned ones. That is why colonial-era laws like 295A, 153A and sedition (124A) survive in India though they no longer exist in Britain, and why challenging them as unconstitutional doesn't work. Ajay adds that the constituent assembly had India's best minds but lacked a theory of the state: the problem was seen simply as getting rid of the white rulers.
core_ideas.quote: I feel that many of these fundamental rights have been framed from the point of view of a police constable.

core_ideas.concept: Power Corrupts Character, Not Just Wallets
core_ideas.explanation: Amit says the founding generation, in government and opposition, were the best and brightest, and men like Nehru were never corrupt for money. But proximity to power breeds arrogance and the belief that you know better than everyone else. The result: a Constitution amended so often that, as Amit recounts, Ambedkar said in the early 1950s he would gladly burn it himself. Amit adds that no party in India is squeaky clean; whoever is in power uses these laws against their enemies.
core_ideas.quote: power doesn't just corrupt in the obvious sense that you want to make more money. I don't think people like Nehru and so on were ever corrupt in that way. Definitely not. But it corrupts character.

core_ideas.concept: Two Failings of the Elites: Infantilisation and Hypocrisy
core_ideas.explanation: Infantilisation means treating citizens as incapable of making their own decisions. Film censorship and talk of 'uplifting the consciousness of the masses' both come from it. Hypocrisy means opposing speech laws when they are used against your side and cheering when they hit your enemies. Amit's prescription for any free speech controversy: don't personalise it ('we don't like him') and don't politicise it. Either way it will come back to hurt society, and creators especially.
core_ideas.quote: Many people who claim to be for free speech are actually for free speech they agree with.

core_ideas.concept: Punish the Act, Not the Speech
core_ideas.explanation: Amit answers the standard objections. Falsely shouting fire in a crowded theatre is already punishable as trespass on the owner's property and as harm or attempted harm to others, so no speech exception is needed. Hurt feelings are subjective and could cover anything; adults should not invoke the coercive power of the state over offence. Ajay adds that India's 'snowflakes problem' reflects insecurity and low self-esteem: why listen to, or read, what you dislike? If hate speech leads to violence, punish the violence, and treat the speaker as an accessory only if there was direct incitement. Libel is for civil courts and damages, not criminal law; India is unusual in treating it as criminal. Fraud, like Ajay's example of a medicine claiming 100mg of salicylic acid that contains 50mg, is fraud, not a speech issue.
core_ideas.quote: If someone commits violence because of something I say, you know, you catch that person and you punish the violence, and that is the end of the matter.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's response to people who think incitement must be defined in black-and-white law: in the common law, judges exist to read subtle situations and decide whether something was humour or a genuine incitement to violence. A workable principle doesn't need a mechanical rule.
core_ideas.quote: the people who are asking for black and white laws are not respecting the glory of the common law and the role of the judges in thinking that does this cross the line.

core_ideas.concept: Free Speech Is a Battle Against the State
core_ideas.explanation: Blocking someone on Twitter, or a platform enforcing terms you agreed to, is not censorship. The state holds a monopoly on violence, and when it silences you, you are silenced everywhere. A private person merely declines to give you space in their home or timeline. Your rights end where they infringe on someone else's property and rules, and no one is entitled to anyone else's attention.
core_ideas.quote: the battle for free speech is fundamentally a battle against the state.

core_ideas.concept: Weak State Capacity Means India Needs More Free Speech, Not Less
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay flips the usual argument that if the UK or Germany has restriction X, India should too. In India, filing a criminal or civil case and going through the courts is itself the punishment, and police, prosecutors and judges don't function well. So until India learns how to make these institutions work, which he puts at the next hundred years, the bar for free speech should be higher than in the West. Amit adds that claiming Indians are too sensitive for free speech insults a society that has managed more diversity than any other, for centuries.
core_ideas.quote: you need even lower restrictions on free speech in India because of the infirmities of the state.

core_ideas.concept: Truth Is Too High a Bar: Finance as a Marketplace of Ideas
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay worries about rules that protect only true statements. Most of the world is a fog of war, and if you could speak only with documentary proof, you would hardly speak at all. Securities and derivatives markets are pure marketplaces of opinion. Treating speculators as unable to sift claims for themselves is infantilisation. Short sellers who take a position and then publish damaging findings about a company are healthy, almost investigative journalism, and they deserve more respect because they put money behind their views. Forcing companies to monitor and rebut every social-media rumour is 'just dumb' and pulls them away from running their business.
core_ideas.quote: if there's a random YouTuber who is dissing Infosys, then you know he's just a random YouTuber. But if the guy is putting his money on the line and actually shorting Infosys, I respect him more.

core_ideas.concept: Every Propaganda Medium Has a Learning Curve
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay credits this idea to their friend Suyash Rai. Each new medium, from Mussolini's radio to film, television, WhatsApp and now LLMs, sets off a moral panic. In 2012-13, WhatsApp felt like an alien spaceship: messages seemed to come from family, and people believed everything. Today nobody believes WhatsApp forwards. For now, a perfectly typeset, grammatical text earns trust, and LLMs are being used to push propaganda that way, but people will learn. Ajay says he is less optimistic about the masses than Amit, yet the remedy is still to let it play out rather than reach for state power.
core_ideas.quote: At every stage, humans can be caught, but you can't fool all the people all the time and there is a learning curve.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: The 'black and white' opener: Amit notes that below the waist both hosts are in black, so Ajay is actually black and white while 'I am black alone.' Later: 'when it comes to shirts, I know you are firmly a white man and I am firmly black.'
Amit says BeerBiceps started out as a fitness channel, which is why he sometimes jokingly calls him 'Tequila Triceps.'

Amit acts out Ranveer's interview trick of repeating your last line back as a question: you say 'free speech is important for a democracy,' and he goes, eyes wide, 'Oh, free speech is important for a democracy?' Then you elaborate for another two minutes.
On the election-season podcast rush: the right-wing podcasters must have thought 'Modi hamare paas aayenge' (Modi will come to us). 'Modiji completely ignored those guys, just went for the numbers.'

On the India's Got Latent editor being booked: 'as young Nomsita would know, an editor's job is to cut things out, and this editor did not cut out the anap-shanap, as it were. Except that if you try to cut out everything that people will find objectionable from a comedy show, you'll basically have nothing left.' (Nomsita edits this show.)

Amit's hate-speech example: saying 'Gujarati economists should not be allowed to speak up' is protected hate speech, as is what Ajay has said about Bengali economists ('all of that, which I agree with, by the way'). The line is crossed only at 'here is Ajay Shah's address, go and lynch him.'

Ajay's test case for incitement: a tweet ordering Amit's 100,000 followers to 'get a glass of cold water and dunk it on Nomsita's head.' His followers, being wise and sensible, know it's humour and no water lands on her head. Deciding such cases is what judges are for.
Introducing the history chapter: 'When life used to be short, nasty, and brutish, the folks endowed with the biceps would hurl a punch at the folks endowed with a silver tongue.'
The cartoon Amit recalls from the early Republic: someone at the parliament bookstore asks for a copy of the Constitution, and the clerk replies, 'I'm afraid we don't stock periodicals.'

On 'decency and morality' as grounds for restriction: if Amit opened another couple of shirt buttons, 'it offends decency and morality. I mean, I might say it myself, actually, frankly, because I know what my chest looks like.'
Amit on hurt feelings: 'We are adults. It's not like we are kindergarten children or Oh teacher, teacher, Ajay hurt my feelings, take away his tiffin box.'

Amit, as Ajay rails against India's snowflakes: 'Oh, is your God so weak that mere words from someone like me can hurt your God?' Ajay adds: 'what kind of omniscient, omnipotent creature can be affected by mere words.'
Sign-off: if you disagree, 'tell us why in the comments, because you have free speech.'
The closing line twists the old slogan 'the revolution will not be televised': 'even if the revolution has all the tools of propaganda at its disposal, the counter-revolution will also be televised.'
Hanlon's razor ('never attribute to malice what can be adequately explained by stupidity'), which Amit applies to Ranveer as perhaps ignorance: 'I don't want to call him stupid.'
Oliver Wendell Holmes's 1919 line about falsely shouting fire in a crowded theatre. Amit notes the judgment was later overturned and argues the scenario is already covered by property and harm laws.
Ambedkar's early-1950s lament, as recounted by Amit: he had been proud of the Constitution, but seeing what was being done to it, 'I would gladly burn it myself.'
Wright's Law, in Ajay's rant about being forced to rebut social-media rumours: a company should be busy getting 'twenty percent gains for each doubling of output', not policing chat groups.
